pos: n. (the mother house of the Carthusian order, founded by Bruno in 1084 in the Chartreuse massif)
etymology: French, the great Chartreuse, from the valley of Chartreuse in Dauphiné; Latin Cartusia.
biblical_def: The Grande Chartreuse stands at a thousand metres in a closed valley of the Chartreuse massif north of Grenoble, and has been the head of the Carthusian order since Bruno settled there in 1084. The present buildings date largely from after the fire of 1676, one of some eight fires and avalanches that have destroyed the house; the great cloister is the longest in France, running past the separate cells of the fathers. The monks have made the liqueur since the eighteenth century from a recipe only two of them know, which funds the order. No visitors are admitted. This dictionary records the Grande Chartreuse for the silence it keeps, because stillness in Scripture is commanded in a particular connection. It is the posture before God himself, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). It is the whole earth's proper attitude, “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). It is where Elijah finally heard what he came for, “and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12), and it is where strength is said to be found, “in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines silence as forbearance of speech; stillness as freedom from noise; quietness as rest or repose; solitude as a lonely life; and a cell as a small close apartment.
webster_full: SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech; also, stillness; the state of being without sound.
STILLNESS, n. Freedom from noise or motion; calmness; quiet; silence.
QUIETNESS, n. A state of rest; stillness; calmness; freedom from agitation or alarm; tranquillity; peace.
SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; also, a lonely place; a desert.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the cave or hut of a hermit.
scriptures: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
corruption_summary: Mother house of the Carthusians, 1084: eight times destroyed by fire and avalanche, rebuilt each time, and closed to visitors still.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture commands stillness and attaches it to knowing God rather than to emptying the mind, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). Habakkuk makes it the creation's proper posture rather than a technique, “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). Modern life is loud and the correction is biblical, not merely monastic.

The qualification is in Elijah's case, which is the passage most often cited and most often truncated. He did not go to the mountain for silence; he went in despair, and the silence was the setting in which a voice spoke and gave him orders, “and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12). The quietness Isaiah commends is likewise a confidence in someone, and the verse ends with Israel refusing it, “in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15). Silence is a room, not an answer.

pos: n. (the Lombard charterhouse founded in 1396 by Gian Galeazzo Visconti as a dynastic mausoleum)
etymology: Italian certosa, a charterhouse, from Latin Cartusia; of Pavia in Lombardy.
biblical_def: The Certosa di Pavia was founded in 1396 by Gian Galeazzo Visconti, duke of Milan, as a Carthusian monastery and as the burial church of his dynasty. It is the most lavish charterhouse ever built: a marble facade of inlaid panels and medallions, frescoed vaults, a great cloister of a hundred and twenty-two arches, inlaid wood, and the duke's own tomb. The contradiction is complete and was obvious at the time, since the Carthusian statutes forbade ornament of any kind. This dictionary records the Certosa for that contradiction, because Scripture addresses the use of magnificence in worship with more care than either side of the argument usually allows. God commanded a splendid tabernacle, down to the gold and the blue, and filled craftsmen to make it. Yet he refuses the premise that he is housed or enriched, “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24). The question put to a builder of a temple is where it could possibly be, “where is the house that ye build unto me?” (Isa 66:1). And the thing he actually looks at is named, “to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word” (Isa 66:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines magnificence as grandeur of appearance; marble as a hard calcareous stone used in sculpture; a mausoleum as a magnificent tomb; ornament as that which embellishes; and austerity as severity of life.
webster_full: MAGNIFICENCE, n. Grandeur of appearance; greatness and splendor of show or state; as the magnificence of a palace or of a procession.
MARBLE, n. A calcarious stone of a firmer texture than limestone, and susceptible of a polish; used in sculpture and architecture.
MAUSOLEUM, n. A magnificent tomb, or stately sepulchral monument.
ORNAMENT, n. That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
scriptures: God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
Isa 66:1
Thus saith the LORD, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?
Isa 66:2
For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the LORD: but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Lombard charterhouse of 1396: a duke's marble mausoleum built for an order whose own statutes forbade ornament.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture is not simply against splendour. The tabernacle was commanded in gold and fine twined linen, and the men who made it were said to be filled with the Spirit for the work. So a bare building is not automatically more faithful than a beautiful one, and iconoclasm has its own self-congratulation.

What Scripture does refuse is the idea that God is lodged or enriched by what we build. Paul says it to the most architecturally confident city in the world, “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24), and Isaiah puts the question in a form that makes the whole project look small, “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” (Isa 66:1). He then names what God does attend to, and it is not marble, “to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word” (Isa 66:2), which Micah had already reduced to three things, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). A duke's tomb in a silent order's church answers none of them.

pos: n. (the Tuscan charterhouse of 1338, whose monks were shot in 1944 for sheltering fugitives)
etymology: Italian farneta, an oak wood, from farnia, the common oak.
biblical_def: The Certosa di Farneta near Lucca in Tuscany was founded in 1338 and is still a Carthusian house. In 1944, with the German front passing through, the monks sheltered Jews, escaped prisoners of war and Italian refugees inside the enclosure, hiding some thirty or forty people in the cells and outbuildings. On the first of September the SS surrounded the house; the prior Dom Gabriele Costa and other monks and guests were taken, and twelve of them, including the prior, were shot or died in custody in what is remembered as the Farneta massacre. This dictionary records Farneta because Scripture commands exactly the act for which these men died. The duty to intervene for the condemned is stated as a command with the excuse pre-refused, “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11). The rescue of the helpless is a charge, “Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked” (Psa 82:4). Handing over the fugitive is named as a crime, “neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress” (Oba 1:14), and the fear that silences such men is addressed directly, “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to deliver as to rescue from danger; a refugee as one who flees for safety; to shelter as to protect from injury; to betray as to deliver into the hands of an enemy; and courage as bravery in facing danger.
webster_full: DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue from danger, evil or bondage.
REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.
SHELTER, v.t. To cover from violence, injury, annoyance or attack; to protect; to defend; to harbor.
BETRAY, v.t. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; to disclose with a breach of trust.
COURAGE, n. Bravery; intrepidity; that quality of mind which enables men to encounter danger and difficulties with firmness.
scriptures: If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
Psa 82:4
Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.
Oba 1:14
Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: Tuscan charterhouse of 1338: in 1944 its monks hid Jews and escaped prisoners, and twelve of them including the prior were shot.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture makes rescue a duty rather than a heroism, and it anticipates the excuse. Solomon addresses the man who would rather not be involved and gives him no room, “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11), and the psalm puts it as a plain order, “Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked” (Psa 82:4).

Obadiah supplies the opposite case and treats it as a crime of the first order: standing at the crossway and handing over those who had escaped, “Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape” (Oba 1:14). Against the calculation that makes a man do that, the Lord gives the only argument that answers it, “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28). Twelve men at Farneta were shot because they had done the commanded thing; an enclosed order had understood something a great many free men did not.

pos: n. (the Nottinghamshire charterhouse of 1343, whose prior was among the first martyrs of the English Reformation)
etymology: Norman French beau val, the fair valley; Latin Bellavallis.
biblical_def: Beauvale in Nottinghamshire was founded in 1343 by Nicholas de Cantelupe and was one of only nine English charterhouses. In 1535 its prior, Robert Lawrence, travelled to London with Augustine Webster of Axholme to ask Thomas Cromwell how the Carthusians were to deal with the Oath of Supremacy; they were arrested, tried with John Houghton of the London house, and on the fourth of May 1535 all three were hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn in their habits, the first religious to die in Henry's breach with Rome. Fragments of the priory stand on a farm. This dictionary records Beauvale for the question they came to ask, because an oath is a serious matter in Scripture and a conscience bound by one is not being obstinate. The Lord restricts swearing sharply, “Swear not at all” (Mat 5:34), and sets the standard for speech instead, “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37). James repeats it as a command, “swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth” (Jam 5:12). And a confession made or refused before men is weighed, “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father” (Mat 10:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God; to swear as to affirm with an appeal to God; supremacy as the state of being supreme; conscience as the internal judgment of right and wrong; and a martyr as one who suffers death for his faith.
webster_full: OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed; the appeal to God in an oath implies that the person imprecates his vengeance if the declaration is false.
SWEAR, v.i. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
MARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who suffers death in defense of any belief.
scriptures: Mat 5:34
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jam 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Nottinghamshire charterhouse of 1343: its prior went to London to ask how to answer the Oath of Supremacy and was quartered at Tyburn in 1535.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an oath is not a formality. The Lord's restriction is severe precisely because swearing invokes God as a witness, and he replaces the whole apparatus with simple truthfulness, “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37). James, writing to Christians, repeats it without softening, “swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath” (Jam 5:12).

This dictionary is confessionally Protestant and does not hold that the pope is head of the church; three Carthusians died in 1535 for a claim it does not share. What it will not do is pretend the question was trivial or the men cowards. They asked, in advance and in person, how a conscience could swear what it did not believe, and when no answer came they refused and took the consequence. The Lord's own weighing of such a moment is not about which side was right but about whether a man speaks, “whosoever shall deny me before men” (Mat 10:33). The principle to recover is that an oath you do not mean is a sin whatever the government wants.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire charterhouse of 1397 on the Isle of Axholme, later the scene of the fen drainage riots)
etymology: From the town of Haxey with Old Norse holmr, an island in a marsh.
biblical_def: The charterhouse of the Visitation of St Mary was founded in 1397 at Low Melwood on the Isle of Axholme, an area of raised ground amid the Lincolnshire fens. Its prior Augustine Webster was executed at Tyburn in 1535 with the priors of Beauvale and London. In the 1620s Cornelius Vermuyden drained Hatfield Chase and the surrounding levels under a grant from the crown, and the commoners of Axholme, whose rights of pasture and turbary went with the water, rioted, broke the works and litigated for decades. This dictionary records Axholme for that long quarrel over boundaries, because the removal of a landmark is one of the few property offences Scripture names repeatedly and curses. The command is blunt, “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark” (Deu 19:14). Solomon repeats it twice, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28), “Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10). Job lists it among the works of the wicked, “Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof” (Job 24:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; a boundary as a limit; a common as land held in common by a community; to encroach as to enter on the rights of another; and drainage as the act of draining land.
webster_full: LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object; as a marked tree, a stone, a ditch, or a heap of stones, by which the limits of a farm or other portion of land are designated.
BOUNDARY, n. A limit; a bound; that which marks the extent of a possession or a territory.
COMMON, n. An open ground, or that soil the use of which belongs equally to the inhabitants of a town or of a lordship.
ENCROACH, v.i. To enter on the rights and possessions of another; to intrude; to take possession of what belongs to another, by gradual advances.
DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to pass through some porous substance; to empty by drawing off gradually, as a marsh.
scriptures: Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless:
Job 24:2
Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof.
corruption_summary: Lincolnshire charterhouse of 1397 on a fen island: its prior died at Tyburn, and its commoners spent decades fighting the drainage of their commons.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how seriously Scripture treats a boundary. A landmark was a stone in a field, and moving it at night transferred land without anybody appearing to steal anything, which is exactly why the law names it, “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set” (Deu 19:14). Solomon repeats the command and attaches it, the second time, to the defenceless, “and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10).

The second thing is the company such an act keeps in Scripture. Job lists the moving of landmarks in the same breath as driving off flocks and oppressing the poor, as the ordinary business of men who prosper by it, “Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof” (Job 24:2). The drainage of Hatfield Chase was good engineering and enriched a crown and a contractor by extinguishing the rights of people who had no deeds; a village that rioted for sixty years had read its Proverbs, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28).

pos: n. (the Yorkshire charterhouse of 1398, the best preserved in England)
etymology: From the dedication Mons Gratiae, the mount of grace; founded as the House of the Assumption and St Nicholas.
biblical_def: Mount Grace at Osmotherley in North Yorkshire was founded in 1398 by Thomas de Holland, duke of Surrey, and is the best preserved of the nine English charterhouses. The great cloister with its cells is legible on the ground, and one cell has been reconstructed with its two rooms, its workshop and its walled garden, together with the hatch through which food was passed without a word. The house surrendered in 1539. This dictionary records Mount Grace for its name, because grace is the word the whole Carthusian project most needed and could least supply by rule. It is the ground of salvation and it is explicitly not earned, “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). It outruns sin rather than matching it, “where sin abounded, grace did much more abound” (Rom 5:20). It has appeared to everyone rather than to a vocation, “For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men” (Tit 2:11), and it is approached at a throne by the needy, “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited love and favour of God; favour as kind regard; merit as desert or worthiness of reward; a gift as something bestowed without price; and salvation as deliverance from sin.
webster_full: GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart and restrains from sin; a state of reconciliation to God.
FAVOR, n. Kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition; a kind act or office.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward; worth; excellence deserving honor or reward.
GIFT, n. A present; any thing given or bestowed; any thing the property of which is voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation.
SALVATION, n. The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death, and the conferring on him everlasting happiness.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 5:20
Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound:
Tit 2:11
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Heb 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
corruption_summary: Yorkshire charterhouse of 1398, the mount of grace: the best preserved in England, with one cell rebuilt down to the hatch for the food.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the dedication. Grace in Scripture is defined against earning, and Paul makes the exclusion twice in one sentence so that no reader can fit anything of his own into it, “and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). A charterhouse named the mount of grace was built by men who then spent their lives attempting to climb it.

The second thing is the scale and the access. Grace is not a quantity to be matched against a man's record; it is described as outrunning the worst of it, “where sin abounded, grace did much more abound” (Rom 5:20). It has appeared to all men rather than to the professionally religious, “hath appeared to all men” (Tit 2:11), and the way to it is a throne a needy man may approach without a mediator in a habit, “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16). The hatch in the cell door is a parable nobody meant.

“where sin abounded, grace did much more abound” (Rom 5:20) — not a quantity to be matched.
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16) — access without a hatch.

pos: n. (the Provencal charterhouse of 1117, among the oldest Carthusian houses still inhabited)
etymology: From Occitan, the hill of the stream; mont, a hill, with riu, a brook.
biblical_def: Montrieux lies in a wooded valley of the Massif de la Sainte-Baume in Provence and was founded in 1117, thirty-three years after the Grande Chartreuse itself, which makes it one of the oldest Carthusian houses still occupied. It was burnt by the Wars of Religion, suppressed at the Revolution, bought back by the order in the nineteenth century, and emptied again by the French anticlerical laws of 1901 before the monks returned. It is closed to the public, and its guest cells are used by men making retreats. This dictionary records Montrieux for its persistence, and because a nine-century stretch of ordinary days is the setting Scripture puts most of its promises in. The faithful are told to continue, “If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled” (Col 1:23). Endurance is the mark rather than intensity, “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13). Weariness in doing good is anticipated and forbidden, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap” (Gal 6:9), and the long work is promised not to be wasted, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to persevere as to persist in a design begun; to endure as to last or continue; constancy as firmness of mind; to continue as to remain in a state; and patience as the suffering of afflictions with calmness.
webster_full: PERSEVERE, v.i. To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken; to pursue steadily any design or course commenced; not to give over or abandon.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue; to remain; to bear; to brook; to sustain without breaking or yielding.
CONSTANCY, n. Firmness of mind; stability; steadiness; particularly, firmness in adhering to a cause or to principles.
CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely; to be permanent or durable; to last.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
scriptures: Col 1:23

If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Provencal charterhouse of 1117: burnt, suppressed, emptied and reoccupied across nine centuries, and still closed to visitors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's characteristic word to believers is continue. It is not an exciting instruction, and it is the one most often given, “If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled” (Col 1:23), with endurance rather than intensity named as the mark of the genuine, “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13).

The second thing is that weariness is expected. Paul does not tell the Galatians that good work is energising; he tells them not to quit when it stops being so, and attaches a harvest with no date on it, “for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9). His closing word on the resurrection chapter is addressed to people doing unglamorous work with no visible result, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). Nine hundred years of a house burnt and refilled is what that looks like from outside.
roots_summary: Greek epimeno (G1961), to continue in; Greek hupomeno (G5278), to endure; Greek ekkakeo (G1573), to grow weary; Greek kenos (G2756), empty, in vain; Greek themelioo (G2311), to ground.
roots_lines: Greek epimeno (G1961) — to remain in, to continue; “If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled”, Colossians 1:23.
Greek hupomeno (G5278) — to bear up under, to endure; “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved”, Matthew 24:13.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to be weary; “let us not be weary in well doing”, Galatians 6:9.
Greek ekluo (G1590) — to faint, to give out; “if we faint not”, Galatians 6:9.
Greek kenos (G2756) — empty, void of result; “your labour is not in vain in the Lord”, 1 Corinthians 15:58.
usage: “If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled” (Col 1:23) — the least exciting and most repeated instruction.
“for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) — a harvest with no date on it.
“your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — addressed to unglamorous work.

pos: n. (the charterhouse of 1204 in the Lazio mountains, founded by Innocent III)
etymology: From Latin tres saltus, the three leaps or passes, of the mountain tracks above Collepardo.
biblical_def: Trisulti stands high above Collepardo in the Lazio mountains, on a site where an earlier Benedictine house had stood near the cave of Dominic of Sora. Innocent III founded the charterhouse in 1204, and it was Carthusian until 1947, when Cistercians took it over. The buildings are fortress-like, walled against the mountain, with an eighteenth-century pharmacy decorated in trompe-l'oeil and a library of some thirty-six thousand volumes. This dictionary records Trisulti for the shape of the place, because a fortified refuge in the mountains is a figure Scripture uses and then redirects. The Name itself is called the stronghold, “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). God is named a tower in the same breath as a rock and a fortress, “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2). He has been the shelter in fact, “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psa 61:3), and Jerusalem's surrounding hills are read as a picture of him, “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people” (Psa 125:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fortress as a fortified place; a tower as a lofty building; a stronghold as a place of security; a rock as a large mass of stony matter; and a refuge as shelter from danger.
webster_full: FORTRESS, n. Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a strong hold; a place of defense or security.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories; a citadel; a fortress.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort; a fortress; a place of security.
ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals; also, defense; means of safety; protection.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.
scriptures: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Psa 61:3
For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
corruption_summary: Lazio charterhouse of 1204, founded by Innocent III: a fortress against the mountain, with a painted pharmacy and thirty-six thousand books.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the redirection Scripture performs on the image. Everyone understands wanting a fortress; the proverb takes the wish and puts the tower somewhere a wall cannot be built, “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). David piles the words up, rock, fortress, deliverer, because no single one of them is adequate, “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2).

The second thing is that the claim is made in retrospect by men who had actually been hunted. David is not describing a theory, “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psa 61:3). And the psalm of ascents turns the physical geography of a walled city into a statement about God rather than about masonry, “so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever” (Psa 125:2). A house built against a mountainside is reading the right figure; the figure points past the mountain.
roots_summary: Hebrew migdal (H4026), a tower; Hebrew 'oz (H5797), strength; Hebrew metsudah (H4686), a fortress; Hebrew machaceh (H4268), a shelter; Hebrew cela' (H5553), a rock.
roots_lines: Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower, here the Name; “The name of the LORD is a strong tower”, Proverbs 18:10.
Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run, into the tower; “the righteous runneth into it, and is safe”, Proverbs 18:10.
Hebrew metsudah (H4686) — a fortress, a fastness; “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer”, Psalm 18:2.
Hebrew machaceh (H4268) — a shelter, proved in fact; “For thou hast been a shelter for me”, Psalm 61:3.
Hebrew cabib (H5439) — round about, encircling; “so the LORD is round about his people”, Psalm 125:2.
usage: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower” (Pro 18:10) — the tower moved where no wall can be built.
“The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2) — three words because one will not do.
“As the mountains are round about Jerusalem” (Psa 125:2) — geography read as theology.

pos: n. (the Swabian charterhouse of 1402, whose carved choir stalls were sold to England and bought back)
etymology: German Buchs, the box tree, and Heim, a home; the box-tree dwelling.
biblical_def: Buxheim near Memmingen in Swabia became a charterhouse in 1402 and was the only Carthusian house in the imperial circle of Swabia. Its choir stalls, carved by Ignaz Waibl between 1687 and 1691, are among the great works of German baroque woodcarving. After the abbey was dissolved in 1803 the stalls were sold in 1883 to an English buyer and spent nearly a century abroad; they were bought back in 1980 and reinstalled. This dictionary records Buxheim for the box tree in its name, because the box appears in Scripture in two promises about replanting a wasteland, and both are about what God supplies rather than what grows naturally. Trees are named for the desert, “I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19). The same three are promised for the sanctuary, “The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together” (Isa 60:13). The purpose is given, “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together” (Isa 41:20), and the planter is named, “that the hand of the LORD hath done this” (Isa 41:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines box as an evergreen shrub or tree with hard wood; to carve as to cut into shapes with a chisel; a stall as a seat in a church choir; timber as wood fit for building; and to graft as to insert a shoot into another stock.
webster_full: BOX, n. A shrub or tree of several species, of hard close-grained wood, much used by engravers and turners; the boxwood.
CARVE, v.t. To cut into some particular form; to engrave; to cut figures or devices on hard materials, as wood or stone.
STALL, n. A seat; a bench; also, a seat in the chancel of a church, appropriated to a dignitary.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture, carriages, fences, ships and the like.
GRAFT, v.t. To insert a shoot or scion of one tree or plant into another for propagation.
scriptures: I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
corruption_summary: Swabian charterhouse of 1402: its Waibl choir stalls were sold to England in 1883 and bought back nearly a century later.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that both of Isaiah's box-tree promises are about planting where nothing grows. The trees are set in a desert rather than a nursery, and the list is deliberately specific, “I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19). The same species reappear as the furnishing of a restored sanctuary, “to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13).

The second thing is the stated purpose, which is not horticultural. The planting is done so that observers will draw a conclusion about who did it, “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this” (Isa 41:20). The same note sounds in the promise that a desert will bloom, “and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1). Carved boxwood returning after ninety-seven years to the choir it was cut for is a small instance of a thing being restored to its place, which is what the whole image is about.

roots_lines: Hebrew te'ashshur (H8391) — the box tree, named twice; “and the pine, and the box tree together”, Isaiah 41:19.
Hebrew 'arabah (H6160) — a desert plain, the planting site; “I will set in the desert the fir tree”, Isaiah 41:19.
Hebrew pa'ar (H6286) — to beautify, of the sanctuary; “to beautify the place of my sanctuary”, Isaiah 60:13.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to understand, the stated purpose; “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together”, Isaiah 41:20.
Hebrew yad (H3027) — the hand that did it; “that the hand of the LORD hath done this”, Isaiah 41:20.
usage: “I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19) — planted where nothing grows.
“to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13) — the same species, furnishing a temple.
“that the hand of the LORD hath done this” (Isa 41:20) — the conclusion the planting is for.

pos: n. (the Thurgau charterhouse sacked and burnt by a reforming mob in 1524)
etymology: From a Germanic personal name with the settlement ending -ingen.
biblical_def: Ittingen in the Thurgau was an Augustinian house that became a charterhouse in 1461. In July 1524 a crowd from the surrounding villages and from Zurich territory, stirred up by preaching against the mass and by a local grievance over an arrested preacher, broke into the charterhouse, drank the cellar dry, burnt the archives and the library and set fire to the buildings. The Ittinger Sturm became a political crisis for Zurich, which had to disown and punish the rioters, and it is one of the uglier episodes of the Swiss Reformation. The house was rebuilt and survived until 1848. This dictionary records Ittingen because the sin it illustrates is a Protestant one and the correction is biblical. Zeal without knowledge is named, “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). Haste is condemned in the same terms, “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Pro 19:2). Men will do violence thinking it service, “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and the Lord rebuked disciples who wanted fire from heaven, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines zeal as passionate ardour in pursuit of an object; a riot as a tumultuous disturbance by an unlawful assembly; iconoclasm as the breaking of images; sacrilege as the violation of sacred things; and rashness as the quality of acting without due deliberation.
webster_full: ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this word is used in a good sense, but it may denote enthusiasm or ardor in a bad cause.
RIOT, n. In a general sense, tumult; uproar; hence technically, a tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by an unlawful assembly of three or more persons.
ICONOCLAST, n. A breaker or destroyer of images; one who attempts to reform without regard to established usages.
SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religious uses.
RASHNESS, n. The quality of being rash, or of acting or speaking without due deliberation; precipitation; inconsiderate haste.
scriptures: Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
Joh 16:2
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
corruption_summary: Thurgau charterhouse sacked and burnt by a reforming mob in 1524, in an episode Zurich itself had to disown and punish.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Paul credits his opponents with real zeal and still calls them wrong, which is the only honest way to describe the Ittinger mob, “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). Solomon states the general rule about acting faster than one understands, “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Pro 19:2).

The second thing is how convincing such violence feels from inside. The Lord warns that persecutors will be sincere, “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and he turned on two of his own disciples when they proposed to burn a Samaritan village in his name, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). A Reformation whose doctrine this dictionary holds produced, on one July night in the Thurgau, a drunken mob burning a library. The principle to recover is that the rightness of a cause does not sanctify its methods.
roots_summary: Greek zelos (G2205), zeal; Greek epignosis (G1922), full knowledge; Hebrew 'uts (H213), to hasten; Greek latreia (G2999), service; Greek epitimao (G2008), to rebuke.
roots_lines: Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, real but misdirected; “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.
Greek epignosis (G1922) — knowledge, the missing thing; “but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.
Hebrew 'uts (H213) — to press, to hasten; “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth”, Proverbs 19:2.
Greek latreia (G2999) — religious service, sincerely offered; “will think that he doeth God service”, John 16:2.
Greek epitimao (G2008) — to rebuke, as he rebuked them; “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of”, Luke 9:55.
usage: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — zeal credited and still called wrong.
“will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) — how convincing it feels from inside.
“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55) — said to his own disciples.
